notes.body:
The ميثاق — the pledge of loyalty and obedience — is formally taken with the living Imam through the summoner (داعي), his appointed representative. Entering it is not agreeing to a list of rules but **a living bond between the soul and its spiritual guide**. Everything listed — prayer, moral conduct, obedience — is daily evidence that this bond holds.

This is why each act listed breaks the covenant. Abandoning prayer without excuse, committing fornication, killing a believer, or refusing to believe a fellow believer's oath — **each tears the fabric of the community** that the ميثاق is meant to weave together and protect, each an act of withdrawal from a solemnly contracted relationship.

The ميثاق is rooted in something far older — the primordial agreement in which every soul bore witness before Allah:

وَإِذْ أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ مِن بَنِى ءَادَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ ۖ قَالُوا۟ بَلَىٰ ۛ شَهِدْنَآ

And when your Lord took from the children of Adam — from their loins — their descendants and made them testify: 'Am I not your Lord?' They said, 'Yes, we have testified.'
Al-A'raf 7:172

This original pledge is **renewed in every era through the living Imam**, who holds the believer accountable to it in their time.

The instruction about striving with person and wealth at the summoner's command brings this into sharpest focus. The داعي does not issue personal orders — he relays the Imam's guidance, and **refusing him without excuse is refusing the Imam himself**. Breaking the covenant is the severance of the soul's living connection to the Imam's light.

notes.quote: whoever abandons the prayer without excuse, or abandons any of the prescribed works, has broken the covenant
etymology: ميثاق (covenant): from the root و-ث-ق, meaning to be firm, secure, and to bind tightly. Related words: وثيقة (a binding document) and وثيق (firm, strong). The ميثاق is literally something that holds you fast — not just a promise spoken once, but a tie that fixes the believer to something larger than themselves.

داعي (summoner): from the root د-ع-و, meaning to call, to invite, to summon. Related words: دعوة (mission or call) and دعاء (supplication). The داعي is literally 'the one who calls' — the root captures exactly his role: to bridge the believer and the Imam by drawing souls toward the light of guidance.

عهد (covenant, agreement): from the root ع-ه-د, meaning to commit, to know closely, to entrust. Related: عاهد (one who covenants) and معهد (institute or place of covenant). The عهد is not signed once and set aside — it is something continuously remembered and lived, which is why abandoning its terms is treated as an active breach.

notes.body:
The Ismaili method of inner interpretation (تأويل) peels back the surface of a word to reveal the truth it was always pointing toward — its hidden reality (باطن) beneath its outward form (ظاهر). This is what happens when the hadith

تارك سنتي ملعون
The one who abandons my sunnah is cursed.

is read as pointing to the legatee — not a creative departure, but a return to what the words actually carry. The word ملعون, from the root ل-ع-ن, means one who has been **driven to the far distance** — expelled, cut off. "Banished from the mercy of Allah" is therefore a linguistically exact rendering, not a loose paraphrase.

The key lies in the word سنة itself. From the root س-ن-ن — to lay down a path, to set something in continuous flow — a سنة is not a collection of habits but a living way that must be carried forward. In Ismaili understanding, the one appointed to carry the Prophet's way forward across time is the legatee (وصي), Maulana Ali. Abandoning the legatee is therefore **abandoning the sunnah at its living source**.

This is reinforced through the structure of prayer, which divides into two kinds: obligatory and sunnah. In Ismaili doctrine, the Prophet and the legatee are always a pair — the speaking one (ناطق) who declares the revelation, and the preserving one (وصي) who holds its inner reality. The obligatory prayer corresponds to the Prophet's revelation; the sunnah prayer corresponds to the legatee. **The sunnah dimension of religion is the legatee dimension** — to abandon one is to abandon the other. Maulana Ali's own words confirm this:

لا حظ في الإسلام لمن ترك الصلاة
There is no portion in Islam for the one who abandons the prayer.
notes.anchor: the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed. Meaning: the one who abando…
notes.quote: the one who abandons my sunnah is cursed. Meaning: the one who abandons my legatee is one banished from the mercy of God
etymology: سنة (sunnah): from the root س-ن-ن, meaning to lay down a path, set something flowing, or to smooth and shape a course. سنة is an established way — worn into being by repeated motion. The root captures something that must be actively kept moving to stay alive; without a carrier, a سنة simply ceases to flow.

ملعون (the banished one): from the root ل-ع-ن, meaning to drive away, to expel to the outer boundary. ملعون is not vaguely 'cursed' — it is one who has been cast out, severed, pushed to the extreme far edge. 'Banished from the mercy of Allah' is therefore a linguistically exact reading, not an interpretive addition.

تأويل (inner interpretation): from the root أ-و-ل, meaning to return to the beginning, to bring something back to its first origin. تأويل traces a word or act back to the original truth it emerged from — not projecting meaning in, but following meaning home. The root tells us that every outward form has an originating reality it came from.

وصي (legatee): from the root و-ص-ي, meaning to join, connect, or to bequeath by binding one thing to another. A وصي is the one to whom something is entrusted at the moment of transmission — the one who receives the Prophet's trust and holds the chain unbroken. The root itself is a description of continuity.

notes.body:
When the people of Shuayb ask whether his prayer commanded them to abandon their fathers' worship, they are treating **the outward act of worship** as though it were itself the source of moral command — demanding that visible movements justify themselves as an authority.

The outward (الظاهر) is contrasted with the inward (الباطن) — the distinction running through all Ismaili thought about worship. الظاهر is the visible form: the movements, the words, the postures. الباطن is **the living reality those forms are meant to carry**:

- the soul's recognition of the Imam of the Time
- the walaya (الولاية) flowing from him
- the genuine submission that reshapes a person from within

It is this inward reality that **truly commands and forbids**, because it acts upon the heart and not merely on the body.

The hadith cited just before the Shuayb passage makes this unmistakable:
مَنْ لَمْ تَنْهَ صَلَاتُهُ عَنِ الْفَحْشَاءِ وَالْمُنْكَرِ لَمْ يَزْدَدْ مِنَ اللَّهِ اِلَّا بُعْدًا
Whoever is not restrained by his prayer from indecency and wrongdoing increases in nothing but distance from Allah.

**A prayer without its inward meaning** does not transform the person — it only repeats the same movements, accumulating distance rather than closeness.

Shuayb's people could only see the shell; they could not perceive the prophetic guidance animating his worship from within. الظاهر is real and obligatory, but it is a vessel. The **living walaya** (الولاية) is what the vessel carries, and that is what truly commands the soul.
notes.anchor: it is because the outward prayer neither forbids nor commands
notes.quote: it is because the outward prayer neither forbids nor commands
etymology: ظاهر (outward, manifest): from the root ظ-ه-ر, meaning to rise to the surface and appear plainly. الظاهر is literally what shows itself — the visible face of a thing. The root also gives ظهر (the back), which faces outward by nature. In worship, الظاهر is everything the prayer presents to the eye.

باطن (inward, hidden): from the root ب-ط-ن, meaning belly or interior. الباطن is what lives in the belly of a thing — concealed beneath the surface. The root gives بطن (abdomen), suggesting depth and hiddenness. In worship, الباطن is the inner reality the form carries but cannot itself make visible.

صلاة (prayer): from the root ص-ل-و, carrying the sense of connection and following closely. Prayer is a living link between the servant and Allah. Some linguists trace it to صَلَا (the lower back), since bowing and prostration involve that part of the body, binding physical movement to inward submission.

الولاية (walaya, guardianship and proximity): from the root و-ل-ي, meaning nearness, closeness, and taking charge. الولي is one who is both close to someone and entrusted with their care. الولاية combines intimate nearness with legitimate authority — not mere loyalty, but a living bond carrying the Imam's divine guidance to the believer's soul.

notes.body:
The twelve sunnahs (سنة) of prayer (صلاة) form a **complete structural system** — not a loose collection of extras, but a precise count that must balance across every prayer type. A two-cycle prayer (ركعة) has only one sitting — the final one — so the "first sitting" simply does not exist in its structure. Without something to fill that slot, the count falls to eleven, and the قنوت steps in exactly there.

The **first sitting** in a four-ركعة prayer is a deliberate mid-prayer pause: the worshipper sits after the second cycle and recites the تشهد — a verbal act of witness before Allah. The قنوت performs that same act: hands raised, voice lowered, the worshipper addresses Allah in extended supplication. Same inner movement, different posture.

What makes them **structurally equivalent** is what they share:

- Both are deliberate, worded moments of address to Allah beyond the main recitation
- Both interrupt the physical rhythm of bowing and prostrating with a pause of inner presence
- Both are سنة elements — not the bare minimum for a valid prayer, but what makes it whole

This is why prayers with two sittings carry no قنوت — the first sitting **already occupies that slot**. The system is exact; each prayer type assembles its twelve سنة elements differently but always arrives at the same total.

In Ismaili thought, every physical act of worship reflects an inner reality. The first sitting and the قنوت are two expressions of the same spiritual moment: the point where the worshipper makes **direct, personal address** to Allah — not in prescribed recitation, not in communal praise, but in a voice entirely their own. That functional identity is why one can stand in for the other.

notes.quote: every prayer in which there is no first sitting has a qunut that stands in its place in the count
etymology: قنوت: from the root ق-ن-ت, meaning to be obedient, to remain devoutly standing. The root carries sustained, humble compliance before a master — inner and physical at once. From it comes قانت (the devoutly obedient one). The قنوت is that posture made verbal: a standing of quiet, worded submission directed entirely at Allah.

تشهد: from the root ش-ه-د, meaning to witness, to be present, to testify. The شاهد is one who was there and can attest. The verb form تشهّد means 'he bore witness.' In the prayer's sitting, the worshipper تشهّد — formally declares their faith before Allah — turning a moment of stillness into an act of conscious, personal testimony.

ركعة: from the root ر-ك-ع, meaning to bow, to bend the back in deference. The ركوع — the bowing — is the act that defines a ركعة, so the full cycle of standing, bowing, and prostrating takes its name from that single gesture of submission. A prayer of two ركعات has fewer cycles, which is why its structure differs.
